evidence.assay_type: Human patch test (with photopatch test component)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Concentration: 10.0% w/w; Finn Chamber, occlusion for 2 days; one set irradiated with 10 J/cm² UVA; readings on day 2, 3, 7.
evidence.support_text: In the human patch test study, octocrylene (10.0% w/w, Table 1) induced positive reactions in 5 subjects (8.5% of 60).

evidence.assay_type: Human patch test (with photopatch test component)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Concentration: 2.0% w/w; Finn Chamber, occlusion for 2 days; one set irradiated with 10 J/cm² UVA; readings on day 2, 3, 7.
evidence.support_text: In the human patch test study, methyl methacrylate (2.0% w/w, Table 1) induced positive reactions in 1 subject (1.7% of 60).

evidence.assay_type: Human patch test (with photopatch test component)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Concentration: 5.0% w/w; Finn Chamber, occlusion for 2 days; one set irradiated with 10 J/cm² UVA; readings on day 2, 3, 7.
evidence.support_text: In the human patch test study, 2-ethylhexyl salicylate (5.0% w/w, Table 1) induced positive reactions in 2 subjects (3.4% of 60).

evidence.assay_type: Human patch test (with photopatch test component)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Concentration: 5.0% w/w; Finn Chamber, occlusion for 2 days; one set irradiated with 10 J/cm² UVA; readings on day 2, 3, 7.
evidence.support_text: In the human patch test study, homosalate (5.0% w/w, Table 1) induced positive reactions in 4 subjects (6.8% of 60).

evidence.assay_type: Human patch test (with photopatch test component)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Concentration: 5.0% w/w; Finn Chamber, occlusion for 2 days; one set irradiated with 10 J/cm² UVA; readings on day 2, 3, 7.
evidence.support_text: In the human patch test study, propylene glycol (5.0% w/w, Table 1) induced positive reactions in 10 subjects (16.9% of 60).

evidence.assay_type: Human patch test (with photopatch test component)
evidence.experimental_conditions: Concentration: as is (neat product); Finn Chamber, occlusion for 2 days; one set irradiated with 10 J/cm² UVA; readings on day 2, 3, 7.
evidence.support_text: In the human patch test study, the sunscreen product itself (broad-spectrum sunscreen containing Licochalcone-A) induced positive reactions in 14 subjects (23.7% of 60). The product was applied 'as is' (see Table 1).

evidence.assay_type: human patch test and intracutaneous test
evidence.experimental_conditions: Patients photoallergic to chlorothiazides were tested with patch and intracutaneous tests, both with and without irradiation.
evidence.support_text: In contrast to the sulfanilamides, when patients known to be photoallergic to chlorothiazides were skin tested to the oxidation product 4-amino-6-chlorobenzenedisulfonamide, no positive reactions were elicited in patch and intracutaneous tests and in irradiated patch and intracutaneous tests with this compound (20). Therefore, the exact mechanism by which drugs like chlorothiazides induce skin sensitization remains to be investigated.

evidence.assay_type: human patch test and intracutaneous test
evidence.experimental_conditions: Patients photoallergic to chlorothiazides were tested with patch and intracutaneous tests, both with and without irradiation.
evidence.support_text: In contrast to the sulfanilamides, when patients known to be photoallergic to chlorothiazides were skin tested to the oxidation product 4-hydroxy-amino-6-chlorobenzenedisulfonamide, no positive reactions were elicited in patch and intracutaneous tests and in irradiated patch and intracutaneous tests with this compound (20). Therefore, the exact mechanism by which drugs like chlorothiazides induce skin sensitization remains to be investigated.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 12.5% OTNE in alcohol SDA 39C; 0.1 ml on 1 cm² semi-occlusive patch for 24 h; duplicate sites; one site irradiated with UVA+UVB (three times MED) using Xenon Arc Solar Simulator (290–400 nm); six applications over 3 weeks; challenge patch after 10 days with UV 320–400 nm; reactions read at 15 min, 24, 48, and 72 h after irradiation.
evidence.support_text: A photoallergy test with OTNE (12.5% in alcohol SDA 39C) was conducted on 28 human volunteers using a semi-occlusive patch with duplicate sites, one irradiated with UVA+UVB. After six applications and a challenge patch, no photoallergic effects were observed, as stated in the text: 'No photoallergic effects were observed.'
Musk ambrette has been reported as a photoallergen in humans, with the suggestion that under the influence of light it can be converted to a more potent derivative.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Induction: 6 occlusive applications of 0.15 g test substance over 3 weeks, each 24 h, followed by 2 MEDs UVB + 4 J/cm² UVA. Challenge: 18 days later, 24 h occlusive patch, then one site exposed to 0.5 MED UVB + 4 J/cm² UVA, other site unexposed as irritation control. Scoring at 24, 48, 72 h.
evidence.support_text: A photoallergenicity study of a lipstick containing 1% Glyceryl Rosinate was conducted in 26 human volunteers. Induction involved six occlusive applications over 3 weeks with UV exposure (2 MEDs UVB and 4 J/cm² UVA). Challenge was performed 18 days later with a 24 h occlusive patch and exposure to 0.5 MED UVB and 4 J/cm² UVA at one site, while the other site served as an irritation control. No reactions were observed at any test or control site, indicating that the lipstick did not elicit a photoallergic response (Biosearch, Inc. 1992b).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 103 fair-skinned subjects; induction and challenge phases with UV irradiation; protocol same as previous studies
evidence.support_text: A sunscreen product containing 74.5% SD Alcohol 40 (denatured with Brucine Sulfate) was evaluated for photoallergy among 103 fair-skinned subjects. All reactions to the test material were scored as normal skin, and it was concluded that the test product did not induce photoallergy (CTFA 1999b).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 29 fair-skinned subjects; 0.2 g gel per patch on volar forearm or back; twice-weekly induction for 3 weeks (6 patchings); challenge patch after 2-week rest; UVA irradiation for 17 min (320-400 nm), UVB irradiation duration based on MED (280-320 nm)
evidence.support_text: A gel formula containing 29% SD Alcohol 40-B was evaluated for dermal photoallergy in human subjects. At challenge, no reactions occurred on either the irradiated or the nonirradiated test material sites, and the gel formulation did not induce dermal photoallergy (Harrison Research Laboratories, Inc. 2002b).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 30 subjects (33 initial, 3 dropouts not due to test material); 0.2 g spray liquid per patch; same protocol as gel study: 6 induction patchings over 3 weeks, challenge after 2-week rest; UVA peak 369 nm/17 min; UVB peak 313 nm/time based on skin type and MED
evidence.support_text: A spray liquid formula containing 12% SD Alcohol 40-B was evaluated for dermal photoallergy in human subjects. At challenge, no reactions occurred on either the irradiated or the nonirradiated test material sites, and the spray formulation did not induce dermal photoallergy (Harrison Research Laboratories, Inc. 2004c).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Patches containing neat concentrations of a leave-on body lotion containing 1–5% BTC applied to human volunteers with Fitzpatrick skin types I, II, or III; phototoxicity phase (10 subjects), photoallergy phase (27 subjects); induction and challenge phases.
evidence.support_text: Patches containing neat concentrations of a leave-on body lotion containing 1–5% BTC were applied to human volunteers. In the photoallergy phase (27 subjects), no reactions were observed on the irradiated or non-irradiated test material contact sites or the irradiated control site during the challenge phase. Therefore, the BTC-containing body lotion did not induce a dermal contact photoallergy response.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.1% triclosan in methanol or 2.5% triclosan in petrolatum applied to skin for 1 hour, followed by irradiation from a light source.
evidence.support_text: In two of the studies, concentrations of triclosan at 0.1% in methanol or 2.5% in petrolatum were applied to the skin for 1 hour, followed by irradiation from a light source (Kligman, 1969; Urbach, 1973). No evidence of erythema, photosensitization, or photoallergy was reported in these studies.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 2% triclosan applied to the skin of volunteers for 24 hours before irradiation with UV-A unfiltered light.
evidence.support_text: Wennersten et al. (1984) applied 2% triclosan on the skin of volunteers for 24 hours before irradiating the site with ultraviolet (UV)-A unfiltered light. Results indicated that 2 of the 745 volunteers tested showed a positive photoallergic reaction to triclosan.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Compounds tested from 0.001% to 1% on the back, patches removed at 24 h, one series irradiated with 7 J UVA, readings at 24, 48, and 96 h.
evidence.support_text: Table 3 shows the results in 4 patients with proven contact sensitivity to various lichen compounds in different dilutions. A clear-cut photoallergic reaction could not be provoked by any of the 4 lichen compounds.

evidence.experimental_conditions: cosmetic formulations containing rosinated color additives up to 9.0%; human subjects; 312 subjects; UVA/UVB exposure
evidence.support_text: FDA concluded that the use of rosin as a substratum in color additive lakes is safe, up to rosinated color additive concentrations of 9.0% in cosmetics products. This conclusion was based on the observation that no skin sensitization or photoallergic reactions to cosmetic formulations containing rosinated color additives at concentrations up to 9.0% were noted in human subjects. The human data included a photoallergy test using 312 subjects (FDA 1994b).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Dilutions 0.001% to 1%, patches removed at 24 h, one series irradiated with 7 J UVA, readings at 24, 48, 96 h.
evidence.support_text: A clear-cut photoallergic reaction could not be provoked by any of the 4 lichen compounds.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human subjects; gel formula containing 29% SD Alcohol 40-B
evidence.support_text: A gel formula containing 29% SD Alcohol 40-B and a spray liquid containing 12% SD Alcohol 40-B did not induce photoallergy or dermal sensitization in human subjects. Also, these two formulas did not induce a dermal phototoxic response in humans.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Induction phase: 25% DEP in ethanol applied twice a week for 3 weeks; challenge phase: 25% DEP in ethanol applied under occlusion for 24 h; irradiation with 16 J/cm² UVA and 0.75 MED UVB after patch removal; reactions evaluated at 1, 24, 48, 72 h
evidence.support_text: A human photoallergy test was conducted with diethyl phthalate (DEP). Induction involved 25% DEP in ethanol applied twice a week for 3 weeks with UVA/UVB irradiation. Challenge involved 25% DEP in ethanol under occlusion for 24 h followed by UVA (16 J/cm²) and UVB (0.75 MED) irradiation. There was no evidence for photoallergy in 29 volunteers (26 female, 3 male) (RIFM, 1997a) or in another group of 23 volunteers (15 female, 8 male) (RIFM, 1997b).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% neat; 25 volunteers; 40 mg applied to a 2 cm² site and occluded
evidence.support_text: Acetyl tyrosinamide tested at 1% neat in a human photocontact allergenicity assay with 25 volunteers (40 mg, 2 cm² site, occluded) showed no photocontact-sensitizing potential.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% piroxicam in petrolatum, applied in duplicate under occlusion (Finn Chambers), one row irradiated with 15 J/cm² UVA at 2 days, evaluated at 1 and 2 days after irradiation
evidence.support_text: Photopatch tests with 1% piroxicam in petrolatum showed positive reactions (++ or +++) in the same patients as 10% piroxicam, with the same pattern (Table 1).

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10% piroxicam in petrolatum, applied in duplicate under occlusion (Finn Chambers), one row irradiated with 15 J/cm² UVA at 2 days, evaluated at 1 and 2 days after irradiation
evidence.support_text: Photopatch tests with 10% piroxicam in petrolatum showed positive reactions (++ or +++) in patients 2-5,8-11,17-19, and negative in patients 12,13,15,16 (Table 1). Controls were negative.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 2% cinnamaldehyde in petrolatum, 24 h occluded patch test with Finn Chambers, followed by UVA irradiation (5 J/cm² from Phillips Black light tubes TL 20w/09); reactions read at patch removal and 24 h after irradiation.
evidence.support_text: Sixteen patients were tested with 2% cinnamaldehyde in petrolatum in a 24 h occluded patch test using Finn Chambers. After patch removal, one set was exposed to UVA (5 J/cm²). One allergic reaction was observed, which intensified after irradiation (Thune and Solberg, 1980).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Octocrylene 10% in petrolatum; photopatch test with UVA 5 J/cm² irradiation at day 1; readings at day 2 and day 3 following ICDRG guidelines.
evidence.support_text: Case no. 1: Photoallergologic investigation showed positive reaction to octocrylene, with ++ reaction with and without UVA.

evidence.experimental_conditions: raw material concentration 50%; 200 ppm MIT; occluded dermal patches; 2× MED UVA/UVB; 24-hour application; 6 times over 3 weeks; challenge with 5 µL/cm² and 2 µL/cm²; 10 J/cm² UVA + 0.5 MED UVA/UVB
evidence.support_text: In a study evaluating the photosensitization effects of MIT, 32 subjects were induced and challenged with 200 ppm MIT under occluded dermal patches with UVA/UVB irradiation; no reactions indicating photoallergy to MIT were observed.

evidence.experimental_conditions: tested in 5 patients with thimerosal allergy; materials included mercurial compounds, thiosalicylic acid, and irradiated solution of piroxicam plus L-cysteine
evidence.support_text: 5 patients with allergy to thimerosal and negative photopatch tests to piroxicam were patch tested. In all but one, tests were positive to the mercurial compounds and negative to the other materials, including thiosalicylic acid and the irradiated solution of piroxicam plus L-cysteine.

evidence.experimental_conditions: UV exposure
evidence.support_text: Our case with contact sensitivity to flurbiprofen ... had photocontact allergy to ketoprofen and tiaprofenic acid.

evidence.experimental_conditions: UVA exposure; no concentration or vehicle stated
evidence.support_text: A case of contact photoallergy to PABA was reported in a young English woman who applied a sunscreen containing PABA and experienced a serious generalized rash. Photopatch testing showed positivity only with PABA exposed to UVA light.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Cinnamaldehyde at 0.2%, 1.0% and 2.0% in yellow soft paraffin, closed patch using A1-Test strips for 24 h on upper back, then irradiated with 1 MED solar simulator (xenon arc, 290 nm through visible); reactions read 24 and 48 h after irradiation.
evidence.support_text: In a closed photopatch study, cinnamaldehyde was tested at 0.2%, 1.0% and 2.0% in yellow soft paraffin; patches were applied for 24 h and then irradiated with 1 MED solar simulator. One contact dermatitis patient was tested by the closed procedure and reacted to cinnamaldehyde (Addo et al., 1982).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Cinnamaldehyde at unspecified concentration in yellow soft paraffin, closed patch for 24 h, then irradiated with 1 MED solar simulator; reactions read 24 and 48 h after irradiation.
evidence.support_text: The patient with PLE who did not react in the open application was also tested in the closed patch procedure and then reacted to cinnamaldehyde (Addo et al., 1982).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Cinnamaldehyde in yellow soft paraffin applied openly at ~10 mg/cm² on skin; after 1 h, irradiated with 1 MED solar simulator (xenon arc, 290 nm through visible); reactions read continuously for first 15 min, then at 30 min, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 24 and 48 h.
evidence.support_text: Open application photopatch studies were conducted; cinnamaldehyde was applied directly to the skin (~10 mg/cm²) and irradiated after 1 h. No reactions were observed in 2 out of 2 contact dermatitis patients when tested by open application (Addo et al., 1982).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Same as previous open application conditions: cinnamaldehyde in yellow soft paraffin at ~10 mg/cm², 1 h before irradiation with 1 MED solar simulator.
evidence.support_text: Two patients with polymorphic light eruption (PLE) were tested by open application of cinnamaldehyde; one patient reacted to cinnamaldehyde, while the other did not (Addo et al., 1982).

evidence.assay_type: Human photosensitisation study (HRIPT with UV exposure)
evidence.experimental_conditions: 10% 2-pentylcyclopentan-1-one in petrolatum; 25 human volunteers; induction phase: 10 applications over 24 h each to the same site; 10–14 day rest; challenge patch applied to same and previously unexposed site; UV exposure from Hanovia UV sunlamp for 30 s at 20 in on days 4, 5, 7, 8, 10 induction and challenge; read 24 h after light exposure.
evidence.support_text: A human photosensitisation study (HRIPT) using 10% 2-pentylcyclopentan-1-one in petrolatum on 25 volunteers, with UV exposure during induction and challenge, reported no sensitisation reactions when examined 24 h after light exposure (RIFM, 1978b).

evidence.assay_type: human repeat-insult patch test and photoallergy test
evidence.experimental_conditions: cosmetic formulations containing up to 9.0% rosinated color additives; human subjects; composite of photoallergy test (312 subjects) and repeat-insult patch tests (2381 subjects)
evidence.support_text: FDA concluded that the use of rosin as a substratum in color additive lakes is safe up to rosinated color additive concentrations of 9.0% in cosmetic products, based on observation that no skin sensitization or photoallergic reactions to cosmetic formulations containing rosinated color additives at concentrations up to 9.0% were noted in human subjects. The human data included a photoallergy test using 312 subjects and a composite of repeat-insult patch tests on a total of 2381 subjects.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 10 repeated applications of unspecified concentration of triclosan, followed by UV irradiation.
evidence.support_text: Colgate-Palmolive (1972) reported a minimal reaction in 1 volunteer of 106 tested following 10 repeated applications and UV irradiation; however, the concentration of triclosan was not specified in the study.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 104 volunteers received 10 applications of 1%, 5%, or 20% triclosan in petrolatum, followed by UV irradiation.
evidence.support_text: In a repeated-patch study in which 104 volunteers received 10 applications of 1%, 5%, or 20% triclosan in petrolatum followed by UV irradiation, no evidence of photosensitization was reported (Marzulli and Maibach, 1973).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Oral administration of 10 mg/kg body wt. 8-methoxypsoralen, followed by UV-A (320-400 nm) irradiation, mice killed 24 h after third application (see Materials and methods).
evidence.support_text: After oral treatment with 8-MOP the mice developed after UV-A irradiation a severe inflammatory reaction in the skin as indicated by the mean increase in ear thickness of 23.70 ± 3.6 × 10⁻² mm, but with only a moderate proliferation response in the ear-draining lymph nodes (LLN-Index of cell counts: 2.32 ± 14.7%). The calculated DI values indicated a photoirritating potential of 8-MOP (DI of 0.21).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Oral administration of 50 mg/kg body wt. olaquindox, followed by UV-A (320-400 nm) irradiation, mice killed 24 h after third application (see Materials and methods).
evidence.support_text: Olaquindox-treated mice showed only a very small mean increase in ear thickness (0.4 ± 0.1 × 10⁻² mm, but a strong proliferation response in the ear-draining lymph nodes (LLN-Index of cell counts, 3.18 ± 18.2%).

evidence.experimental_conditions: PBMC from human buffy coats; stimulation with TNBS-modified antigen-presenting cells; 5–16 h incubation; cell sorting and TCR sequencing.
evidence.support_text: TNBS-specific CD154+CD4+ and CD137+CD8+ memory T cells were sorted from 5 to 16 h experiments, respectively, and their TCR were sequenced. This detection method (AIM assay) identifies chemical-specific T cells based on upregulation of CD154 (CD4+) and CD137 (CD8+).

evidence.assay_type: Adoptive transfer of CD4+ regulatory T cells with CHS readout
evidence.experimental_conditions: The same protocol as for CD8+ T cells, but CD4-positive T cells were isolated from donor mice and transferred to naive recipients; recipients were then challenged with DNFB.
evidence.support_text: Dietary GSPs inhibition of UVB-induced suppression of CHS was associated with diminishment of the development of regulatory CD4-positive T cells. This suggests GSPs reduce regulatory T-cell activity, thereby enhancing the CHS response.

evidence.assay_type: Adoptive transfer of CD8+ effector T cells with CHS readout
evidence.experimental_conditions: Donor C3H/HeN mice were fed GSPs-supplemented or control diet and exposed to UVB before DNFB sensitization. CD8+ T cells were isolated from lymph nodes and injected i.v. into naive recipient mice, which were then challenged with DNFB.
evidence.support_text: In an adoptive transfer experiment, CD8-positive T cells from UVB-exposed and GSPs-fed donor mice induced a greater CHS response in naive recipients than cells from UVB-exposed donor mice not given GSPs. This indicates that GSPs enhance the activity of effector CD8+ T cells.

evidence.assay_type: adoptive transfer of hapten-specific T cells
evidence.experimental_conditions: Hapten-specific Th1 and Tc1 cells isolated from mice sensitized with trinitrochlorobenzene (TNCB) and transferred to naive wild-type mice.
evidence.support_text: Adoptive transfer of hapten-specific Th1 and Tc1 cells from mice sensitized with trinitrochlorobenzene (TNCB) induced strong DTHR (ear swelling) in naive wild-type recipients, confirming that TNCB generates hapten-specific T cells.

evidence.experimental_conditions: PBMC-based; human monocytes and B cells; anti-TNP antibody staining; 10-min reaction time (implicit).
evidence.support_text: Due to its reactivity, TNBS covalently binds to free amino groups within 10 min, including ε-amino groups of lysine-containing peptides presented by MHC proteins on the cell surface. Using an anti-TNP antibody staining, we showed an efficient and reproducible cell surface modification, especially for monocytes and B cells.

evidence.assay_type: antigen-specific in vitro T cell re-stimulation
evidence.experimental_conditions: mice fed control diet for four weeks prior to sensitization; TNCB sensitization; in vitro re-stimulation with antigen
evidence.support_text: Using antigen-specific in vitro T cell re-stimulation and ELISA, we showed an antigen-specific T cell response in the local lymph nodes in high fat diet and control diet fed mice upon TNCB treatment.

evidence.assay_type: antigen-specific in vitro T cell re-stimulation
evidence.experimental_conditions: mice fed high fat diet for four weeks prior to sensitization; TNCB sensitization; in vitro re-stimulation with antigen
evidence.support_text: Using antigen-specific in vitro T cell re-stimulation and ELISA, we showed an antigen-specific T cell response in the local lymph nodes in high fat diet and control diet fed mice upon TNCB treatment.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 3 mM TNBS for APC modification; 16 h incubation; human PBMC; flow cytometry
evidence.support_text: Detection of TNBS-specific T cells by CD137 upregulation on CD8+ T cells after incubation with TNBS-modified APC. Summarized frequencies showed a significant increase (*p < 0.05) of CD137+CD8+ T cells in response to TNBS compared to control. APC modified with 3 mM TNBS.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 3 mM TNBS for APC modification; 5 h incubation; human PBMC; flow cytometry
evidence.support_text: Detection of TNBS-specific T cells by CD154 upregulation on CD4+ T cells after incubation with TNBS-modified APC. Summarized frequencies showed a significant increase (*p < 0.05) of CD154+CD4+ T cells in response to TNBS compared to control (PBS). APC were modified with 3 mM TNBS (chosen as standard concentration in paragraph 32).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human buffy coats, n=11; cells stimulated with TNBS; CD137 and CD69 measured by flow cytometry
evidence.support_text: Among TNBS-specific CD8+ T cells, CD69 co-expression was 64% (mean) for memory T cells (n=11 buffy coats), indicating TCR-mediated activation.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human buffy coats, n=11; cells stimulated with TNBS; CD137 and CD69 measured by flow cytometry
evidence.support_text: Among TNBS-specific CD8+ T cells, CD69 co-expression was 74% (mean) for naive T cells (n=11 buffy coats), indicating TCR-mediated activation.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human buffy coats, n=6; cells stimulated with TNBS; CD154 and CD69 measured by flow cytometry
evidence.support_text: Among TNBS-specific CD4+ T cells, CD69 co-expression was observed at 71% (mean) for naive T cells (n=6 buffy coats), indicating TCR-mediated activation.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human buffy coats, n=6; cells stimulated with TNBS; CD154 and CD69 measured by flow cytometry
evidence.support_text: Among TNBS-specific CD4+ T cells, CD69 co-expression was observed at 82% (mean) for memory T cells (n=6 buffy coats), indicating TCR-mediated activation.

evidence.experimental_conditions: oral gavage, 250 mg/kg cinnamaldehyde, rats, urine analysis
evidence.support_text: In rats, following an oral gavage dose of 250 mg/kg cinnamaldehyde, 15% of the dose was excreted in urine as two mercapturic acids (N-acetyl-S-(1-phenyl-3-hydroxypropyl)cysteine and N-acetyl-S-(1-phenyl-2-carboxyethyl)cysteine, ratio 4:1), derived from direct conjugation of cinnamaldehyde with glutathione. Overall, mercapturic acids represented 6–15% of administered cinnamaldehyde dose in rats and mice.

evidence.assay_type: In vivo glutathione level measurement in liver
evidence.experimental_conditions: Challenge with 50 µL of 0.5% DNCB topically in ACD mice (previously sensitized with 50 µL of 2% DNCB); liver harvested at 24 h post-challenge; Mus musculus model.
evidence.support_text: The amounts of hepatic glutathione decrease after challenge with DNCB in the ACD group was 2.0 µmol, which the authors attribute to conjugation of DNCB with GSH.

evidence.assay_type: In vivo glutathione level measurement in liver
evidence.experimental_conditions: Challenge with 50 µL of 0.5% DNCB topically in ICD mice; liver harvested at 24 h post-challenge; Mus musculus model.
evidence.support_text: The amounts of hepatic glutathione decrease after challenge with DNCB in the ICD group was 1.2 µmol, which the authors attribute to conjugation of DNCB with GSH.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Isolated rat hepatocytes incubated with [¹⁴C]lamotrigine, low turnover rate
evidence.support_text: Isolated rat hepatocytes incubated with [¹⁴C]lamotrigine achieved a low rate of turnover to the glutathione adduct, indicating covalent modification of glutathione.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.6 mM [14C]CDNB, 1.2 µM enzyme, 1.2 mM GSH, 25°C, 15 min, 0.04 M Tris-HCl pH 8.2; protein denatured with 6 M guanidine HCl or trichloroacetic acid precipitation
evidence.support_text: In the presence of GSH, covalently bound CDNB decreased to 1.4 mol per mol of human acidic lung glutathione S-transferase.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 0.6 mM [14C]CDNB, 1.2 µM enzyme, 25°C, 15 min, 0.04 M Tris-HCl pH 8.2; protein denatured with 6 M guanidine HCl or trichloroacetic acid precipitation
evidence.support_text: Incubation of human acidic lung glutathione S-transferase with [14C]CDNB and denaturation resulted in approximately 3 mol of CDNB bound per mol of enzyme in the absence of GSH.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Clinical photopatch testing; patients included those with known ketoprofen photosensitivity and those without ketoprofen use.
evidence.support_text: In a clinical study, 6 patients with positive photopatch test reactions to octocrylene stated they had not used ketoprofen, and none reacted to benzophenone-3. Additionally, all patients with ketoprofen photosensitivity also presented with positive photopatch test reactions to octocrylene. This demonstrates that octocrylene can cause positive photopatch test reactions in humans.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human photopatch testing in patients with ketoprofen history; 15 out of 17 showed positive reactions
evidence.support_text: Fifteen of these 17 patients were also recorded as having a positive photopatch test reaction to benzophenone-3.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human photopatch testing in patients with ketoprofen history; all 17 showed positive reactions
evidence.support_text: These 17 patients were photopatch tested with both ketoprofen and octocrylene, and all showed positive photopatch reactions to both compounds.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Human photopatch testing; 23 patients positive to octocrylene
evidence.support_text: Five of the 23 octocrylene-positive patients reacted in the patch test, whereas 18 patients reacted only in the photopatch test.

evidence.experimental_conditions: photopatch test with piroxicam at 1% and 10% concentrations; patients with thimerosal allergy and piroxicam-induced photosensitivity
evidence.support_text: The 17 patients with allergy to thimerosal were photopatch tested with piroxicam (1% and 10%). Nine had a positive result with both concentrations, while the test was negative in the remaining eight patients and in ten control subjects. Patient nos. 18 and 19, with piroxicam-induced photosensitivity, also had a strong positive test.

evidence.experimental_conditions: UVA irradiation, standard photopatch test procedure
evidence.support_text: Patient no. 19 had a positive photopatch test to piroxicam after developing acute dermatitis following piroxicam therapy. Patient no. 18 also had strong positive photopatch tests to piroxicam.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 2% w/v TEA-Quat in petrolatum; occluded 8 mm Finn Chambers on back for 2 days; read immediately and after 2 days; 183 patients at St John's Institute, London.
evidence.support_text: In diagnostic patch testing at St John's Institute, London, 183 patients were patch-tested with TEA-Quat at 2% w/v in petrolatum; no inflammatory skin reactions were observed at this subirritant concentration.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 5% w/v TEA-Quat in petrolatum; occluded 8 mm Finn Chambers on back for 2 days; read immediately and after 2 days; 183 patients in London and 56 patients in Leuven.
evidence.support_text: In diagnostic patch testing at 5% w/v, 183 London patients showed 31 reactions to TEA-Quat (12 at day 2) judged irritant; 56 Leuven patients had 5 reactions (4 at day 2) judged weak/equivocal irritant. No allergic reactions were attributed to TEA-Quat.

evidence.experimental_conditions: TEA-Quat at 2% concentration; patch test; 183 patients; 2-day scoring.
evidence.support_text: In the diagnostic patch test for TEA-Quat at 2% concentration, the number of skin reactions at 2-day scoring was 0 out of 183.

evidence.experimental_conditions: TEA-Quat at 5% concentration; patch test; 239 patients; first reading time.
evidence.support_text: In the diagnostic patch test for TEA-Quat at 5% concentration, the number of skin reactions in one reading was 16 out of 239.

evidence.experimental_conditions: TEA-Quat at 5% concentration; patch test; 239 patients; second reading time.
evidence.support_text: In the diagnostic patch test for TEA-Quat at 5% concentration, the number of skin reactions in a different reading was 0 out of 239.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Eye lotion containing 1% Cucumis sativus fruit extract, tested neat, HRIPT on 103 patients with 24-hour semiocclusive patches 3 times per week for 3 weeks for induction, challenge after 2-week nontreatment period, evaluated at removal and 48 and 72 hours
evidence.support_text: In a HRIPT on 103 patients, an eye lotion containing 1% Cucumis sativus (cucumber) fruit extract applied neat was concluded to have no potential for eliciting dermal irritation or sensitization.
